description:
Somos un equipo que esta emocionado de participar en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 con el reto Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. Nos apasiona la idea de usar datos reales de la NASA para crear un mapa interactivo que ayude a explorar, entender y moverse por la superficie marciana.

La primera es la vencida :D
summary:
Red Dust: Mars Explorer is a browser-based mission planner that helps an astronaut prepare and run a safe walk on the surface of Mars. We combined NASA data from Viking, MOLA, HiRISE and Mars Trek into a layered map with three views: a flat map, a 3D relief model and a full globe.

The astronaut picks a home base, then chooses from 24 sites: volcanoes, canyons and the Exploration Zones NASA has studied for the first human landing. For each site the app shows real elevation and slope, how much atmosphere sits overhead to block radiation, and how dusty it tends to be. It then plans the smoothest route from the base, avoiding steep ground.

The app also has a crew wellness panel with simulated vital signs and RED DUST AI, a voice assistant that answers questions in English or Spanish without an internet connection.

This matters because on Mars a bad route can end a mission. Turning raw orbital data into simple, clear decisions gives a crew one less thing to worry about when help is millions of kilometers away.
details:
What it does and how it works

Red Dust: Mars Explorer is a mission planning tool for astronauts working on the surface of Mars. It runs in any web browser and is organized into four sections.

  • Home base and Missions. When the app starts, the astronaut sets the location of their home base. They then pick a destination from 24 sites grouped into three categories: volcanoes and mountains, the Exploration Zones proposed to NASA for the first human landing, and other places of interest such as Valles Marineris or the Mars Pathfinder site. Every site has a description, objectives, a timeline, an image from NASA Mars Trek and a safety outlook. That outlook is calculated from real MOLA elevation data: average and maximum slope within 50 km, how much atmosphere sits overhead to shield against radiation, and an estimate of dust opacity.
  • Maps. The route can be explored in three views. The Cartographic view uses NASA Mars Trek tiles, the Relief view is a 3D surface built from MOLA altimetry, and the 3D Globe is built on Esri and USGS planetary services. The app plans the smoothest route from the base to the destination with a pathfinding algorithm that avoids steep ground, then splits it into waypoints. The rover can drive the route and return to base.
  • Wellness. A crew panel with a 3D astronaut and vital signs. These readings are simulated and clearly labeled as such.
  • RED DUST AI. An assistant that answers questions about Mars, geology and route safety, and opens any section by voice or text, in English or Spanish. Its knowledge base lives in the browser, so it does not depend on any external AI service.

Benefits and expected impact

On Mars, a bad route can cost energy, equipment or lives. Orbital data already exists, but it is spread across many tools and hard to read quickly. Red Dust turns that data into a few clear answers: where to go, how steep it is, how exposed you are and how to get back. The same tool also works for students and the public who want to understand why some places on Mars are safer than others, and why NASA is looking at specific landing zones.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, built with Vite.
  • Graphics and maps: Three.js for the 3D relief, the home globe and the astronaut. Leaflet for the flat map. ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript for the 3D globe.
  • Data: NASA Mars Trek WMTS tiles, MGS MOLA elevation data (processed with our own Node.js scripts), USGS/IAU planetary nomenclature, and abstracts from NASA's 2015 Exploration Zone workshop.
  • Voice: Web Speech API for speech recognition and speech output.
  • 3D model: "Astronaut" by Jungle Jim (CC BY 4.0), in glTF format.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. Everything was built and tested on regular laptops and phones.

What makes it creative

Instead of showing raw maps, we built the tool around one question an astronaut would actually ask: "Is it safe to go there, and how do I get back?" Every screen leads to that answer. We also mixed real science with a mission control feel, from the boot sequence to the voice assistant, so the data is easier to use under pressure.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and honesty: coordinates, elevations and site descriptions come from real NASA and USGS sources. Anything simulated, like the vital signs or EVA hours, is labeled. The assistant never makes up sensor readings.
  • Reliability: if online map services fail, the app falls back to local data and a simpler globe, so it keeps working.
  • Accessibility: keyboard navigation, screen reader labels, support for reduced motion and two languages.
  • Performance: routes thousands of kilometers long are computed in a fraction of a second, and the app also works on phones.
